stages.name: Poverty and inequality
stages.title: Poverity and inequality
stages.sub: Evaluate whether capitalism's tendency towards inequality is offset by state action.

steps.q: Country A takes 20% of everyone's income in tax, whatever they earn. Does this narrow the gap between a low earner and a high earner?
steps.right: No, the gap stays the same in proportion
steps.wrong: Yes, the gap becomes much smaller
steps.hint: If both pay the same percentage, does the poorer person end up relatively better off compared to the richer one?

steps.q: Now compare that flat-rate country to one that taxes high earners more heavily and pays benefits to the poorest. Does that second country end up with a smaller gap between rich and poor?
steps.right: Yes, the gap ends up much smaller
steps.wrong: No, the gap stays exactly the same
steps.hint: Think about who keeps more of their income after tax and transfers in each country.

steps.q: Capital naturally builds up faster than wages grow, pulling incomes apart over time. If a government then taxes that capital heavily and gives the money to low earners, does that pull the gap back together?
steps.right: Yes, it pulls the gap back together, at least partly
steps.wrong: No, it makes the gap grow even faster
steps.hint: Does state action here work in the same direction as the wealth-concentrating mechanism, or against it?

steps.q: One country lets capital accumulate freely and redistributes almost nothing. Another has the same capitalist system but taxes capital heavily and redistributes it. Will both countries end up equally unequal?
steps.right: No, the redistribution changes how unequal each ends up
steps.wrong: Yes, both end up exactly as unequal as each other
steps.hint: Is inequality under capitalism fixed, or does it depend on what the state does on top of the underlying system?
